summary: Overall quality is high. Every numeric key, worked example and table figure was recomputed independently in Python (shear angle, friction angle, Taylor and economic tool life, Chvorinov and riser sizing, upset force, rolling draft, extrusion, wire drawing, blanking, bend allowance, blank diameter and draw force, heat input, cooling rate, carbon equivalent, restrained stress, PM density and compaction force, LPBF and DED build rates, Cp/Cpk/ppm tails, RSS tolerance stacks and all break-even figures) and all match the keys within tolerance. Cp/Cpk and defect-rate keys use one consistent definition (z = 3*Cpk, one-sided normal tail); rule-of-thumb formulas (0.7*UTS, F = pi d t UTS (D/d - 0.7), mu^2 R, 1.25 riser factor, K-factors, Taylor exponents, arc efficiencies) are all flagged as typical or approximate, and cost figures in the casting, additive and process-selection units are labelled illustrative. No tab or control characters, literal \uXXXX text, '[object Object]' or garbled non-Latin characters were found (packets are pure ASCII). One misleading summary statement in the weld heat-flow unit needs correction; the remaining issues are minor wording, consistency and display-rounding points. This is an AI review only; the course still needs a subject-matter expert before engineering reliance.

issues.problem: Summary bullet 4 says "A weld section shows fusion zone, HAZ (melted-and-changed, unmelted-but-changed) and unaffected parent metal." The HAZ is by definition base metal that did NOT melt; the melted-and-changed region is the fusion zone. This contradicts the lesson body and keys of q001 and q007.
issues.suggestedFix: Reword to: "A weld section shows the fusion zone (melted and re-solidified), the heat-affected zone (not melted but microstructurally changed) and unaffected parent metal."

issues.problem: The maximum-draft worked example hot-rolls strip with mu = 0.12. Typical hot-rolling friction coefficients are higher (roughly 0.2 to 0.5 or more); 0.12 is a cold-rolling-type value, and the unit's own cold-rolling question uses 0.08. The arithmetic (3.6 mm, 30 percent) is correct.
issues.suggestedFix: Either call the example cold rolling or use a representative hot-rolling value (for example mu = 0.25 with R = 250 mm gives about 15.6 mm), and state that the value is illustrative.

issues.problem: In the Cpk-to-ppm table the row for Cpk = 1.33 lists z = 4.00 but gives 0.00330 percent and 33 ppm. Q(4.00) is 31.7 ppm; 33 ppm corresponds to z = 3.99 (3 x 1.33). The 1.67 row likewise shows z = 5.00 with 0.27 ppm, which is Q(5.01).
issues.suggestedFix: Show z as 3.99 and 5.01, or state that z is rounded and that the ppm figures use the unrounded 3 x Cpk.

issues.problem: Wear-limited run-length example: margin 0.035 mm at 0.004 mm growth per part is 8.75, and the answer says "About 8 parts ... the ninth part would exceed the limit". If the first part is made at 39.985 mm, part 9 is 40.017 mm and part 10 (40.021) is the first to exceed, so the count depends on an unstated convention.
issues.suggestedFix: State whether 39.985 mm is the first part or the setting before part 1 (growth applied per part made), and make the answer consistent (8 or 9 parts).

issues.problem: Marking guide asks for a diameter tolerance of "a few micrometres (a tolerance grade around IT5 or IT6)". For a 45 mm diameter IT5 is about 11 micrometres and IT6 about 16 micrometres, which is more than "a few".
issues.suggestedFix: Say "about 10 to 16 micrometres (IT5 to IT6)", or drop the grade reference.

issues.problem: Worked example concludes that a draw ratio of 1.91 "is below 2.0, a single draw is feasible", but the lesson gives LDR as 1.8 to 2.0, so 1.91 lies inside the uncertain range and is not clearly safe.
issues.suggestedFix: Say a single draw is marginal-to-feasible and depends on the actual LDR of the sheet; the check should be against the material's measured LDR.

issues.problem: The explanation says a larger diameter gives "a lower rev/min but a longer path per turn". The cutting path length is L/f regardless of diameter; the real reason is that for fixed V the spindle speed N = 1000V/(pi D) falls as 1/D, so t = L/(fN) rises in proportion to D. The "longer path per turn" phrasing is confusing.
issues.suggestedFix: Explain via t = L/(fN) with N proportional to 1/D at constant cutting speed, so t is proportional to D.

issues.problem: Explanation says a larger shear angle shortens the shear plane "so less metal is sheared per unit time". At fixed speed and feed the removal rate is unchanged; what falls is the shear-plane area and the shear strain, hence the force.
issues.suggestedFix: Replace with: the shorter shear plane has less shear area and lower shear strain, so the cutting force and specific energy fall.

issues.problem: "A lathe spindle motor draws 6.0 kW at the shaft ... drive train is 80 percent efficient ... cutting power at the tool is 80 percent of the motor power." Power "drawn at the shaft" and "motor power" are mixed, so it is unclear whether 6.0 kW is electrical input or shaft output.
issues.suggestedFix: Say the machine draws 6.0 kW of input power and 80 percent reaches the cutting zone; the key of 4.0 J/mm^3 is then correct.

issues.problem: Compaction-force worked example gives "outside diameter of 60 mm" and a "pressing area of 1500 mm^2"; a full 60 mm disc is about 2827 mm^2, so the 60 mm is unused and slightly confusing for a student.
issues.suggestedFix: Remove the diameter or say the part has a central hole/boss relief giving a net projected pressed area of 1500 mm^2.

issues.problem: Unlike the casting, additive and process-selection units, this unit's worked examples (unit-cost breakdown, 60 000-unit die, 1000-part break-even) and numeric questions carry no statement that the cost figures are illustrative. The table also lists overhead as "fixed or allocated" while the worked example and c = F/N + v treat it as a per-part variable charge.
issues.suggestedFix: Add a short note that all currency figures are illustrative, and clarify that machine-hour overhead is charged per part in the variable term while any lump-sum overhead belongs in F.
